The United States moved to force TikTok's sale or ban it primarily due national-security concerns regarding potential Chinese government access to US user data and the platform's algorithm, as determined during CFIUS review [Source: ev-1]. This concern led President Biden to sign the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act on 2024-04-24, which mandated that ByteDance divest TikTok's US operations within roughly 270 days (extendable by 90) or face a ban in the US [Source: ev-1].

The dispute was resolved through an Oracle-led deal announced on 2025-06-10, rather than an outright sale [Source: ev-1]. Under this agreement, Oracle received approximately a 12.5% stake in TikTok's US operations, with participation from SoftBank and other investors, while ByteDance retained a majority interest [Source: ev-1]. The resolution involved structuring the app as a joint venture under "Project Texas," which kept US user data hosted in Oracle's cloud under US control to address security risks [Source: ev-1]. This process occurred after the Supreme Court upheld the law 9-0 on 2025-17 (per curiam), just before the effective date of 2025-2025; following a brief period where TikTok went dark for roughly 14 hours on 2025/2025, President Trump pledged to pause enforcement and issued an executive order on 20-20 that delayed enforcement for 75 days while final ownership structures were completed through 2025 [Source: ev-1].
